data.title: Lichen sclerosus et atrophicus — viva
data.summary: Connective tissue diseases · 15 viva questions with answers
data.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Lichen sclerosus et atrophicus** (Connective tissue diseases)_

**Q1. What is lichen sclerosus (LS)?**
- Chronic inflammatory, scarring, lymphocyte-mediated dermatosis with a strong predilection for anogenital skin; bimodal in women (prepubertal girls and post-menopausal women); in men mostly uncircumcised adults (balanitis xerotica obliterans)
- Associated autoimmunity (thyroid, vitiligo, alopecia areata; antibodies to extracellular matrix protein 1 — ECM1), Koebner, occlusion by urine in uncircumcised males

**Q2. Clinical features in women.**
- Itch (often severe, nocturnal), soreness, dyspareunia, dysuria, constipation in girls
- Porcelain-white atrophic shiny plaques with cigarette-paper wrinkling, purpura/ecchymoses, erosions, fissures in a 'figure-of-eight' around vulva and anus
- Scarring: resorption of labia minora, burying of clitoris (phimosis of clitoral hood), narrowing of introitus; vagina is spared (unlike LP)

**Q3. Clinical features in men.**
- Whitish sclerotic ring on prepuce, glans, coronal sulcus; phimosis (commonest cause of acquired phimosis), meatal stenosis, urethral stricture, painful erections; perianal involvement rare in men

**Q4. Extragenital LS.**
- ~15–20%: white polygonal flat papules coalescing into atrophic plaques with follicular plugging (delling) on trunk, neck, upper arms, under breasts; usually not itchy; does not carry SCC risk

**Q5. Histopathology.**
- Hyperkeratosis with follicular plugging, epidermal atrophy, basal vacuolar change, broad band of homogenised pale oedematous collagen in the upper dermis (hyalinisation), beneath which a band-like lymphocytic infiltrate

**Q6. Differential diagnosis.**
- Vitiligo (no atrophy/scarring), lichen planus (erosive — vagina involved, Wickham's striae), morphoea (LS–morphoea overlap), mucous membrane pemphigoid (scarring), VIN/ differentiated VIN, extramammary Paget's, child sexual abuse (girls — LS purpura misinterpreted as trauma), lichen simplex, candidiasis

**Q7. What is the malignancy risk?**
- Vulval SCC in ~3–5% of untreated anogenital LS (differentiated VIN pathway, HPV-independent); penile SCC risk also raised; reduced by adequate long-term potent topical steroid therapy
- Lifelong follow-up; biopsy persistent ulcers, thickened, hyperkeratotic or non-responding areas

**Q8. Management.**
- Super-potent topical steroid — clobetasol propionate 0.05% ointment once daily for 4 weeks, alternate days for 4 weeks, twice weekly for 4 weeks, then maintenance 1–2 times weekly long-term (30 g tube lasts ~3 months)
- Emollients/soap substitutes; avoid irritants; topical tacrolimus/pimecrolimus as second line
- Men: circumcision is often curative for penile LS (with steroids); meatal dilatation/urethroplasty for strictures
- Refractory: intralesional steroids, acitretin, PDT, fractional CO2 laser, PRP/fat grafting (experimental)
- Girls: improves around puberty in some but may persist — continue treatment

**Q9. Dermoscopy of lichen sclerosus.**
- White structureless areas, keratotic follicular plugs (comedo-like openings), linear/dotted vessels, purpuric spots, chrysalis structures (white shiny lines on polarised view)

**Q10. How do you follow up anogenital LS?**
- Review at 3 months, then 6-monthly to yearly lifelong; teach self-examination; ensure adequate steroid use (fear of steroids leads to under-treatment); biopsy any persistent ulcer, hyperkeratotic plaque or nodule — differentiated VIN/SCC

**Q11. Pathogenesis of LS in more detail.**
- Autoimmune (anti-ECM1 antibodies in ~70% of women, Th1 cytokines, microRNA-155 up-regulation), genetic (HLA-DQ7), hormonal (low androgen/ oestrogen states — prepubertal, postmenopausal), Koebner (scratching, urine occlusion), possible infection (Borrelia — unproven)

**Q12. Why is circumcision curative in many men?**
- The moist, occluded subpreputial environment with chronic urine exposure drives LS (urine-contact Koebner); removing the prepuce eliminates this trigger — LS confined to prepuce is cured; glans/ meatal disease may persist

**Q13. What is LS in children — key points?**
- Girls 3–7 y: itching, soreness, constipation, dysuria, bleeding/ purpura (can be mistaken for sexual abuse — careful but don't dismiss abuse), figure-of-eight pallor; boys: phimosis
- Treatment same (clobetasol), may improve at puberty but often persists — follow-up into adulthood

**Q14. What is genital LS–LP overlap and differentiation?**
- LP: erosive, involves vagina (LS spares vagina), Wickham's striae at margins, oral involvement; LS: porcelain-white atrophy, figure-of-eight, perianal; overlap occurs — biopsy helps; both treated with clobetasol

**Q15. What is the role of surgery in vulvar LS?**
- Only for complications — perineotomy/ Fenton's procedure for introital narrowing, release of clitoral phimosis/ adhesions, excision of VIN/ SCC; surgery does not cure LS (recurs in grafts)

## Quick spotter facts
- Porcelain-white figure-of-eight atrophy around vulva and anus — LS
- Phimosis in adult male — balanitis xerotica obliterans
- Clobetasol ointment, lifelong follow-up for SCC

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Lichen sclerosus). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._
